items.title: Critical Flicker Fusion Frequency As An Experience-Restricted Constraint On Visual Temporal Resolution: What Does And Does Not Change It
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Natalia D. Rydzenska, Pawel J. Winklewski, Michal W. Blaszczyk-Niezgoda, Anna B. Marcinkowska
items.summary: arXiv:2607.29068v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Experience-dependent plasticity is fundamental to adaptive behaviour, yet the conditions under which basic sensory timing can be modified in adulthood remain poorly specified. Critical flicker fusion frequency (CFFF), the threshold at which flicker is perceived as continuous, is unusually informative here: what fails to change it is as well documented as what does. We argue that CFFF is best characterised neither as non-plastic nor as held near a physiological ceiling, but as modifiable only by a specific class of experience, not by amount. Repeated testing changes it little, and cognitive training without temporal content and incoherent-motion exposure leave it unchanged regardless of duration. By contrast, perceptual-learning paradigms that repeatedly drive early visual processing of transient signals can raise it. The evidence is graded: strongest for task-irrelevant coherent motion temporally paired with task targets, with one-year retention in a small subsample; weaker for contrast and dot-motion training; and, for flicker training, confined to amblyopic eyes starting below typical values. Three qualifications apply: samples are small; the motion and contrast paradigms were assessed with a small foveal stimulus on a macular pigment densitometer, whose equivalence with standard CFFF measurement is unestablished; and a minority of untrained controls show comparable changes. We examine whether the restriction originates at peripheral, thalamocortical, or cortical levels; available data do not adjudicate between them. Functional arguments for such a restriction are offered as rationales, not evidence. Proposed links to working-memory precision and metacognition are stated as predictions; first tests were largely negative.

items.title: Expression of White and Gray Matter Autism Functional Network Connectivity Signatures in Infancy
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Qiang Li, Jingyu Liu, Zening Fu, Armin Iraji, Sarah Shultz, Vince D. Calhoun
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Functional connectivity studies have provided valuable insights into altered brain organization in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, most functional connectivity studies focus exclusively on either gray matter (GM) regions or white matter (WM) tracts and examine specific age groups, rather than investigating their functional interactions across brain development. This limits our understanding of how GM-WM functional interactions evolve developmentally and may obscure important aspects of brain network organization in ASD. We combined integrated WM+GM functional network connectivity (FNC) with brain-wide risk scores (BRSs) to quantify ASD-associated pattern expression in ABIDE I/II and an independent infant cohort. We employed a NeuroMark framework with predefined WM and GM intrinsic connectivity networks templates, to estimate subject-level FNC. First, we identified two distinct patterns of altered WM+GM FNC in ASD: GM-related hypoconnectivity centered on the paralimbic network and WM-GM hyperconnectivity centered on the frontal network. These findings highlight the involvement of higher-order cognitive networks and the importance of WM-GM functional interactions in characterizing ASD-related connectivity alterations. Second, infants with a higher familial likelihood of autism exhibited greater mean expression of ASD-associated FNC patterns than those with a lower familial likelihood, as quantified by BRS. These group-level findings do not establish developmental persistence or predict diagnostic outcomes at the individual level.

items.title: Hyperbolic embedding of higher-order simplicial networks
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Martin Guillemaud, Vito Latora, Mario Chavez
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many biological interactions involve groups rather than pairs, as when several proteins assemble into a multi-protein complex. Simplicial complexes naturally capture these collective interactions. Existing hyperbolic embeddings represent network hierarchy and similarity through a few interpretable coordinates, but rely only on pairwise links: they cannot distinguish three units engaged in a common interaction from three units connected only in pairs. We introduce here the hyperbolic higher-order (HHO) embedding, which embeds a simplicial complex into the Poincar\'e disk, while incorporating its group interactions. The hyperbolic area of the triangle spanned by three interacting nodes then measures how compactly their interaction is represented. Testson synthetic and real-world networks, including a co-authorship network and the protein interaction network of \textit{Escherichia coli}, show that HHO reduces the hyperbolic area of triangles representing simplices relative to those obtained from pairwise network embeddings. HHO also recovers node groups more accurately than pairwise embeddings and a weighted-clique alternative, with performance competitive with Euclidean embeddings, while providing a low-dimensional representation that can be analyzed with the tools of network geometry.

items.title: Explainable AI-Driven Neural Activity Analysis in Parkinsonian Rats under Electrical Stimulation
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Jibum Kim, Hanseul Choi, Gaeun Kim, Sunggu Yang, Eunha Baeg, Donggue Kim, Seongwon Jin, Sangwon Byun
items.summary: arXiv:2502.12471v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by motor dysfunction and abnormal neural oscillations. This study combined graphene-based cortical stimulation with an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) framework to investigate spatial and frequency-related features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals were recorded before and after stimulation and classified using EEGNet and DeepConvNet. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) and DeepLIFT were applied to identify frequency bands and recording channels contributing to the classification. The anatomical locations of these channels were mapped onto a cortical map. XAI analyses were performed separately for each animal to examine individual attribution patterns. Our XAI analysis revealed frequency-band- and region-specific contributions to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Our approach provided complementary insights into the features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation ECoG classification alongside PSD-based analyses. These findings highlight the potential of combining graphene-based cortical stimulation with explainable deep learning to identify classification-relevant features across frequency bands and cortical areas in pre- and post-stimulation recordings.

items.title: Lattice-Based Pruning of Recurrent Neural Networks via Poset Modeling: A Corrected Theory and a Matched-Sparsity Evaluation
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Rakesh Sengupta
items.summary: arXiv:2502.16525v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Magnitude pruning of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) ignores how information flows between neurons. An earlier version proposed to model RNN dependencies as a partially ordered set (poset) and to retain the meet-irreducible elements of its dependency lattice. By Birkhoff's representation theorem, the meet-irreducible ideals of a finite poset are in bijection with its elements, so retaining them retains everything; the critical-set criterion used earlier selects precisely the elements comparable to all others, of which a dense recurrent layer has none. Condensing a thresholded dependency graph into strongly connected components yields a well-defined dependency order, a graded order score and an acyclic pruning rule; for Cohen-Grossberg networks and LSTMs, acyclic pruning makes local stability decompose over modules. For a 128-unit LSTM pruned at matched sparsity on row-wise and chunked sequential MNIST (three seeds, equal training budgets), the original rules remove every recurrent weight or equal random column pruning; the order score is no better than degree, PageRank or norm; trained weights show little directional bias; and imposing acyclicity from initialisation costs 2.1 and 10.5 percentage points at 50% and 90% sparsity. In the networks studied, order structure must be imposed rather than discovered.

items.title: Building functional and mechanistic models of cortical computation based on canonical cell type connectivity
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Arno Granier, Katharina A Wilmes, Mihai A Petrovici, Walter Senn
items.summary: arXiv:2504.03031v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neuronal circuits of the cerebral cortex are the structural basis of mammalian cognition. The same qualitative components and connectivity motifs are repeated across functionally specialized cortical areas and mammalian species, suggesting a single underlying algorithmic motif. Here, we propose a perspective on current knowledge of the cortical structure, from which we extract two core principles for computational modeling. The first principle is that cortical cell types fulfill distinct computational roles. The second principle is that cortical connectivity can be efficiently characterized by only a few canonical blueprints of connectivity between cell types. Starting with these two foundational principles, we outline a general framework for building functional and mechanistic models of cortical circuits. Finally, we show that the compressed and generative representations of connectivity entailed by this framework are particularly amenable to automatic search through gradient-free optimization, providing a concrete first step towards modelling the evolution of functional neural circuits.

items.title: Message interaction dynamics covary with brain volume across mammalian connectomes
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Yan Hao, Hannah Lax, Marc-Thorsten H\"utt, Daniel J. Graham
items.summary: arXiv:2505.15477v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Brain network communication models typically assume that signals propagate independently, despite the high network density and small diameter of mammalian connectomes, where interactions among simultaneously propagating messages are likely. We investigate these interactions using the copy-spread-annihilate (CSA) model, a synchronous Markovian message-passing process in which messages spread through the binarized network while undergoing collision-dependent deletion. Simulations on a large comparative dataset of mammalian connectomes show that CSA dynamics produce robust positively-skewed lognormal distributions of message survival across species. Despite using only binary network topology without spatial embedding, message survival accounts for over half of the variance in brain volume across mammal species and outperforms a broad range of established graph-theoretic measures and an alternative communication model with interacting messages. These relationships persisted when measured paths could not revisit nodes. Degree-preserving switch randomization weakens the relationship between message survival and brain volume, indicating that higher-order structural organization contributes to the observed scaling law. We describe a mechanistic explanation of model dynamics that suggests message creation differences among networks shapes message survival. Together, these findings suggest that interactions among propagating messages constitute an important and underexplored determinant of communication dynamics in mammalian brain networks.

items.title: Perceived vertical and eye level as one orientation process: a closed-form account of the Li-Matin combination rules for egocentric space
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: A. Y. Shavit
items.summary: arXiv:2607.19681v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Li and Matin (2005a, 2005b) reported three regularities of the induced visually-perceived vertical (VPV), the direction judged upright. For small tilts, a peripheral line shifts it nearly linearly with tilt, two lines combine nearly linearly, and mirror-image tilts cancel. Each line votes at twice its angle, weighted by its strength. The votes' vector sum $c_1$ is the first circular moment of the doubled angles; half its angle, $\phi=\tfrac12\arg c_1$, is the induced vertical, a stimulus axis, not the judged upright. This is the orientation order-parameter model (PLUMB). We prove that $c_1$ is, up to a constant factor, the only additive summary of axes (lines without arrowheads) that scales with line strength and turns twice as far as the field rotates. With Li and Matin's own length gain and no per-configuration fit, the model matches their multiline coefficients in-sample. Their data rule out complete summation but not simple averaging for long lines. But a line's effect is fourfold (period $90^\circ$): it reverses past $45^\circ$ (Li and Matin, 2005a; Vingerhoets et al., 2009), and near-horizontal lines shift VPV as near-vertical ones do, which $c_1$ forbids. In a two-harmonic fit to Li and Matin's data, $c_1$ carries an estimated 2--4% of a near-vertical line's slope and a fourfold term the rest. To first order in tilt, for near-vertical segments, the readout equals the committee rule Shavit, Li, and Matin (2026) fit to eight line-array experiments, with its drives read as concentrations. If the half-fields' signals are read as sum and difference, perceived eye level (VPEL) is the difference, recovering Shavit, Li, and Matin's (2013) reversed integration rules; a fourfold term gives the same signals, so this does not single out $c_1$. Re-analysed data (30 observers) show the predicted signs and nulls, an internal check only; the cross-field gain is fitted.

items.title: oracq: A Modular Framework for Implementing and Analyzing Quantum Scientific Computing Algorithms
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Zhao-Yun Chen, Ming-Yang Tan, Guo-Ping Guo
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum algorithms for scientific computing are specified against access models such as block-encodings, sparse oracles, state preparations, and quantum random-access memories. Their concrete realization is deliberately left open, yet it is a research variable that changes both the numerical behavior and the resource cost of the program, so every reported conclusion is attributable to one realization. In this paper, we present oracq, a Python framework that makes this choice a managed and checkable decision. Our claim is linguistic rather than infrastructural. Algorithms are stored as persistent register-level programs whose oracle slots are declared and typed but unimplemented. A separate binding pass links compatible realizations, so one stored algorithm can be re-bound to a gate network, a QRAM-backed table, or compiled reversible arithmetic and compared across them. Typed QRAM resources, a compiler from pure Python numerical formulas to reversible fixed-point circuits, and block-encoding algebra with qubitization and QSVT-style kernels supply the constructions. Two end-to-end workflows exercise the framework, a quantum finite-volume pipeline for the compressible Euler equations and a quantum homotopy-analysis pipeline that lifts nonlinear PDEs to composable linear input models. The verification methodology separates implementation error from method error, and logical resource accounts cover programs before and after binding. The framework is openly available at https://github.com/IAI-USTC-Quantum/oracq.

items.title: Almost-Quantum Correlations Violate Information Causality
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Anandamay Das Bhowmik, Manik Banik
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information causality (IC) posits that communicating m classical bits cannot give the receiver access to more than m bits of information about the sender's independent data. Although IC holds in quantum theory and excludes a broad class of supra-quantum correlations, its validity for the almost-quantum set has remained open. This semidefinite relaxation of the quantum set satisfies nontrivial communication complexity, no advantage for non-local computation, macroscopic locality, local orthogonality, and numerical evidence has suggested that it may also satisfy IC. Here we show that almost-quantum correlations violate IC, and do so without bound. Unlike earlier violations of IC, which rely on biased guesses, ours is driven by zero-error certificates: each is rare but never wrong, carries information linear in its probability, and vouches for many of the sender's bits at once. This establishes a sharp dichotomy: either IC is a valid physical principle that excludes these correlations, or any nonsignalling theory realizing them admits no mutual information obeying consistency, data processing and the chain rule. In the latter case, we discuss why the chain rule is the natural property to relinquish, and how this possibility relates to histories-based formulations and to locality defined relative to the state rather than presupposed in a fixed spacetime.

items.title: An Unbounded Separation of Almost-Quantum and Commuting-Operator Correlations in Zero-Error Communication
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Rafiuddin Gazi, Biswadeep Chatterjee, Jayashree Karmakar, Ram Krishna Patra, Manik Banik, Anandamay Das Bhowmik
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Almost-quantum correlations form the $\mathtt{1+AB}$ level of the Navascu\'es--Pironio--Ac\'in hierarchy. They strictly contain the quantum set, are characterized by a single semidefinite program, arise in Sorkin's quantum measure theory, and satisfy several principles proposed to single out quantum theory. We show that they are nevertheless unboundedly stronger than quantum correlations in a zero-error communication task. Alice and Bob receive labels $s,t\in[N]$, $N\ge3$; after one bit from Alice, Bob must decide whether $s=t$, never erring but allowed to abstain. For every model of quantum correlations, from finite-dimensional tensor products to commuting operators, the optimal worst-case probability of a conclusive answer is exactly $1/N$, the value attained with shared randomness, so the bound does not depend on the resolution of Tsirelson's problem. An explicit family of almost-quantum correlations attains $1/19$ for every $N$. For certificates of equality from binary-outcome boxes, we solve the underlying semidefinite programs in closed form. The almost-quantum optimum equals $N^2/(17N^2-80N+64)$ for $N\ge8$ and tends to $1/17$. The first level of the hierarchy, which coincides with the set singled out by macroscopic locality, attains $N/[8(N-2)]$, which tends to $1/8$; its optimal boxes lie outside the almost-quantum set for every $N\ge5$. For longer messages, entanglement saves at most one bit over shared randomness, whereas almost-quantum correlations reduce the one-way zero-error cost of deciding equality of $n$-bit strings from $n$ bits to at most $13$. The quantum bound also yields a linear witness of post-quantumness on a face of the nonsignalling polytope.

items.title: eCAS: An Orbital Embedding Method for Quantum Computing
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Anna Br\"unisholz, Markus Reiher
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Future fault-tolerant quantum computers will allow us to calculate electronic structures of atomistic systems. However, these systems will be intrinsically limited in size, requiring embedding theories for many systems because of the unfavorable scaling of the number of terms describing the electron-electron interaction in the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian. Quantum embedding theories address this challenge by partitioning a quantum system into a region of interest, the impurity, and its (larger) complement, the environment. However, currently available quantum embedding methods place restrictive demands on near-future quantum computers, such as the need to measure reduced density matrices or the need for repeated evaluations. Here, we introduce the new orbital embedding method eCAS that steers clear of these pitfalls by constructing a multi-CAS problem, the active spaces of which are localized and can be solved independently of each other with any quantum algorithm. This also allows for the development of comparatively simple gradient expressions. eCAS leverages the Schmidt decomposition to construct initial impurity and bath orbitals and augments them with localized environment orbitals, based on a mutual correlation criterion. The mutual correlation criterion makes eCAS systematically improvable without the need for any iteratively determined quantities.

items.title: Loss-aware optimization of realistic GKP gid states
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Michal Matul\'ik, Petr Marek
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Realistic preparation of Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states, the prime candidates for quantum computation with bosonic systems, is inevitably burdened by photon loss. We show how taking this loss into account can lead to more robust quantum states, thereby diminishing its negative influence. Using GKP squeezing as an operational figure of merit, we formulate a loss-aware optimization procedure based on the ground state representation of GKP states. Numerical simulations for square, hexagonal, and asymmetric GKP states show that the optimal preparation generally requires a different initial grid spacing than that of the desired ideal code state. For symmetric and hexagonal lattices, the optimal parameters asymptotically follow the simple scaling relation. The optimized states exhibit better GKP squeezing and greater resilience to losses. These results provide a simple and experimentally relevant strategy for improving realistic photonic GKP state preparation in the presence of known photon loss.

items.title: Distilling Knowledge from Search: Decoder Model Factory for Quantum LDPC Codes
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Anil Bilgin, Wanda Hou, Pranav Srinivas, Yi-Zhuang You
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. GraphMP uses local message passing to keep computation scalable as the decoding graph grows. Guided by its predictions, beam search progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading additional decoding time for lower logical error rates. We develop the decoder model factory as a paradigm for training successive models on experience generated by earlier models during decoding. Model-guided search supplies verified trajectories for knowledge distillation, folding computation spent on decoding into reusable training data. Repeated collection and distillation improve the decoder across generations and adapt its strategy as the noise changes. These results motivate a coupled quantum--classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning renews the models from operating experience. The long-term vision is a scalable decoder model factory that produces high-performance, low-latency decoders and continually adapts them to evolving quantum hardware.

items.title: Helper-assisted quantum sensing with low dressed-state leakage
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Shirwan Abdullah
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a two-qubit sensing protocol in which only a helper qubit is read out. Calibrated loading and unloading encode a transverse signal in the helper's phase, keep leakage out of a selected dressed-state band small, and return the sensor close to its idle ground state. We derive an information bound for a single sensor whose excitation stays below a prescribed budget, and simulate repeated operation with an uncertain coupling and finite-duration resets in a driven open-system model. At the tested settings, finite measurement records support estimation with infrequent resets. A helper flip at zero coupling, combined with a reversal of the coupling sign, suppresses a static helper offset shared across a record while retaining the signal, at a cost of about 27% of the no-offset information of a plain sequence of equal duration. Under slowly varying noise, averaging each cycle's likelihood over the correct noise law removes most of the added bias, and a wrong noise law can worsen the estimate. A selected directly read sensor with ideal controls and repeated nondemolition verification has the higher information rate. Any practical benefit of avoiding direct readout therefore requires a device-specific disturbance model.

items.title: Real-time BP decoding of a high-rate QEC code
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Andreas Kell, Daniel Herr, Daniel Bascones Garc\'ia, Alexandru Paler, Davide Orsucci, Francisco L\'azaro, Francisco Garc\'ia Herrero
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a real-time FPGA decoder for a high-rate $[[512,174,8]]$ 3D product qLDPC code. We construct a circuit-level detector-error model for a compact syndrome-extraction schedule and propose a small parallel ensemble of row-wise serial min-sum decoders with cumulative memory. The decoder matches $\text{BP+OSD-CS}_\text{10}$ accuracy with one core and Relay-BP accuracy with three cores. The FPGA implementation meets the latency budget of neutral-atom and trapped-ion systems. An ASIC implementation would improve the latency, enabling real time decoding even for superconducting systems. At a physical error rate of $p=10^{-3}$, three FPGA devices decode 174 logical qubits with a logical error rate of $5\times10^{-7}$ and effective distance 6. For $p=10^{-4}$, and assuming the number of BP iterations is capped to 30, the decoder's average latency is $5.1\,$\textmu s and its worst-case latency is $97.9\,$\textmu s.

items.title: Analytic level statistics of the quantum Rabi model
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Zi-Min Li, Long-Jie Li, German Sierra, Murray T. Batchelor
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41421v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive an analytic expression for the distribution of level spacings in the quantum Rabi model. At high energies, the spectrum in a fixed parity sector takes the asymptotic form of a uniformly spaced ladder modulated by a decaying oscillation. The alternating sign of this oscillation separates successive spacings into two branches. For a finite window containing many oscillations, counting how often the two branches exceed a given spacing yields an analytic expression for the spacing density at leading order. The oscillation amplitude at the lower end of the window sets the range of spacings, and its value at the upper end fixes the positions of two cusps that form twin peaks. Spacing histograms from exact diagonalization agree with the analytic density, including its spacing range and twin peak positions. At leading order, the same spectral analysis also yields an expression for the ratio of consecutive spacings, a statistic that requires no spectral unfolding. The resulting ratio statistics agree closely with those from exact diagonalization. For windows that continue to contain many oscillations, the spacing and ratio peaks move toward unity at higher energies as the spectrum approaches a uniformly spaced ladder. The same counting approach can be explored in other systems with controlled spectral asymptotics, slowly varying spacing branches, and windows containing many oscillations.

items.title: Time-Domain Multiplexing for Resource-Efficient Heralded GKP State Preparation
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Ke-Ming Hu, Jun-Jie He, Yu-Ze Zhu, Pei-Lin Du, Lin Yang, Hao Tang, Xian-Min Jin
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are key resources for fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, but their conditional preparation via Gaussian boson sampling involves a trade-off between source count and photon-number resolution. Distributing heralding photons across more measured modes reduces the resolution required per mode, yet increases the number of simultaneously operated squeezed sources in fully squeezed spatial architectures. Here, we show that time-domain multiplexing (TDM) can reduce these physical source requirements while preserving GKP state quality. Using an end-to-end differentiable Bargmann framework, we find that TDM circuits reusing one or two squeezed sources achieve fidelities comparable to fully squeezed spatial circuits across several configurations. Selected nine-mode configurations retain fidelities above 0.95 with one photon heralded in each measured mode, mitigating detector resolution demands without a proportional increase in source count. Loss-aware reoptimization further shows that, under the investigated spatial loss models, two-mode TDM maintains fidelities near 0.80 at 1.0 dB per channel, whereas the corresponding spatial benchmarks fall below 0.60. These results demonstrate that temporal reuse provides an effective architectural route for balancing source overhead, detection demands, and state preparation performance in the presence of optical loss.

items.title: PyQLAS: A Quantum-Classical Hybrid Solver Library for Linear Systems
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Meng-Han Dou, Teng-Yang Ma, Chuang-Chao Ye, Zhao-Yun Chen, Guo-Ping Guo
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum algorithms solve a linear system at a cost that grows only polylogarithmically in its dimension, but on present-day hardware that advantage is realised only if the quantum and the classical parts of a solve are apportioned deliberately. We present PyQLAS, a quantum--classical hybrid library for linear systems that exposes this apportionment as a design parameter rather than a fixed assumption. PyQLAS builds three nested solvers around a single variational core---a variational solver, an outer residual iteration, and a Krylov-subspace projection---so that the quantum subroutine can be held at a fixed circuit width while the classical host absorbs the growth of the problem. Around them, the library supplies preconditioning at two independent levels, dimension alignment, checkpointing, and device-budget control, and a solve written against the interface runs unchanged on an exact state-vector simulator, on a local sampler, and on a real superconducting processor. The library is validated on the IEEE 118-bus power flow, a standard test system in which the linear solver is embedded in a classical Newton iteration. There, the iteration converges to the specified tolerance and reproduces the classical reference solution to within $2.3\times10^{-8}$ p.u.\ in voltage magnitude and $3.4\times10^{-6}$ degrees in voltage angle.

items.title: Testing hardware quantum machine learning claims with a null circuit: fill prediction on Binance futures with 129 qubits of an IBM Heron processor
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Muhammad Faryad
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum processors are now used as feature generators for classical models on tabular data. A circuit encodes each record, the device returns expectation values, and a classical model learns from them. A recent report claimed large gains from such features, gains that appeared only on noisy hardware. These claims are hard to check, because a quantum device is not a static function. Its state changes from job to job and from one calibration to the next, and that drift can leak information about the outcome into the features. We propose a five-step protocol for testing claims of this kind. It runs a circuit that carries no data in the same jobs as the real one. It checks whether the hardware leaves a recognizable mark on each job. It compares random and natural assignments of records to jobs, replays the null results under other submission orders, and closes the leak with a job-purged backtest. We apply it, pre-registered, to the HSBC and IBM study of fill probabilities in bond trading, which reported a large hardware-only gain. We use a public analog task and run the study's circuit on a 129-qubit chain of an IBM Heron processor. Under controlled assignment the hardware features give no gain over classical features, and the device reproduces the ideal features about as well as shot noise allows. Yet every job carries a distinct fingerprint. A circuit with no data at all predicts fills well above chance when records are batched by outcome and the same job sits on both sides of the train/test split. Removing that overlap removes the effect. The protocol costs under an hour of processor time and is designed for any hardware feature or kernel pipeline on tabular data.

items.title: Parametric Enhancement of an Optical Spring in a Dark Signal-Recycling Cavity
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Kaido Suzuki, Ryo Iden, Ken-ichi Harada, Kentaro Somiya
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical springs tailor the response of precision sensors. Parametric amplification of the signal field stiffens the spring, extending the precision to higher frequencies. A Michelson interferometer operated at a dark fringe is the most direct way to separate the signal from the carrier for amplification. We experimentally demonstrate such quantum manipulation of the optical spring by placing an optical parametric amplifier in a cavity at the dark port, showing a significant increase of the optical-spring constant with the parametric gain within a factor of four below the oscillation threshold.

items.title: Estimation of Quantum Umlaut Information
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Beomjoon Kim, Donghwa Ji, Kabgyun Jeong
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying correlations is important for understanding how quantum states and channels support information processing. Quantum umlaut information $U$ connects such correlations to reliability in hypothesis testing and certain communication settings, but its known formulas require classical descriptions of the underlying states. To estimate correlations without these descriptions, we introduce measured quantum umlaut information $U^M$ by replacing Umegaki relative entropy with measured relative entropy. Its variational formulation leads to a quantum generative adversarial framework for estimating $U^M$ from measurement statistics of unknown bipartite states and classical-quantum channels. This framework optimizes reference states and measurements without reconstructing the target states or channel outputs. For classical-quantum channels, it also optimizes the input probabilities. We further analyze the relation between $U^M$ and $U$, deriving a state-dependent gap bound and characterizing equality for full-rank bipartite states. Numerical simulations show trained estimates close on average to independently computed numerical references for $U^M$ across the tested states and channels. These estimates could help assess how well quantum memories preserve correlations and how noise or drift affects input-output dependence in quantum transmitters and state-preparation devices.

items.title: Optimality of the Petz-Fuchs Smoothed State
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Kiarn T. Laverick
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum state smoothing is an estimation technique that uses past and future measurement information obtained from a continuous-in-time measurement record to reconstruct the state of an open quantum system. Recently, there has been a new approach to quantum state smoothing based on quantum retrodiction known as the Petz-Fuchs smoothed state. Here I prove that this Petz-Fuchs smoothed state majorizes all other smoothed states that only depend on the filtered state (the operator conditioned on the past measurement record) and the retrofiltered effect (the operator describing the future measurement record). To do this, I characterize the set of all possible smoothed states satisfying this condition.

items.title: Anomalous superradiant phases in a quantum Rabi zigzag chain under a synthetic gauge field
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Jun-Bo Tang, Lin-Jun Li, Bin Wei, Yu-Yu Zhang
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the phase diagram of a one-dimensional quantum Rabi zigzag chain under an artificial gauge field, which is implemented via phase-modulated next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) hopping. For a system size of $N=8$, we analytically determine the order parameters and critical thresholds, identifying five distinct superradiant phases. For strong nearest-neighbor (NN) coupling, the system exhibits either a ferro-superradiant (FSR) or an antiferro-superradiant (AFSR) phase depending on its sign. Increasing NNN coupling induces a stripe antiferro-superradiant (sAFSR) phase with antiparallel NNN and parallel NN displacements, which is distinct from the conventional AFSR phase. Tuning the magnetic flux drives the system into chiral or antichiral superradiant phases with opposite ground-state photon currents, which are different from the conventional superradiant phases. Remarkably, geometric frustration within each triangular plaquette stabilizes chiral phases even at small magnetic flux while suppressing the sAFSR phase, which vanishes for $N=6$. Mapping the system onto an effective magnetic Hamiltonian yields an analogous phase diagram featuring distinct magnetic phases, offering insight into the anomalous superradiant phases. This equivalence establishes a quantum optical platform for simulating chiral magnetism.

items.title: Biorthogonal universal quantum control
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Chen-yi Zhang, Jun Jing
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As a paradigm for describing open-quantum-system dynamics, the non-Hermitian Schr\"odinger equation generally modifies state norms, complicating coherent control over the system's Hilbert space. With a general instantaneous frame spanned by biorthogonal ancillary bases, we develop a biorthogonal quantum-control theory for discrete-variable systems governed by time-dependent non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. In particular, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for extracting the transitionless pathways that transport parallel in ket and bra states. When this condition is satisfied by a set of projectors constructed with biorthogonal basis states, the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian becomes diagonal in the relevant biorthogonal subspace, enabling arbitrary initial state to evolve as a superposition of controlled transitionless passages. We further identify the parametric constraints under which the transformation linking the initial and final states becomes unitary. As a result, the final system state is automatically normalized even though the transitional dynamics is nonunitary. Our theory is justified by the bidirectional population transfer and a holomonic quantum gate implemented by a non-Hermitian three-level system in $\Lambda$ type. For the population transfer, controlled gain and loss reduce the required coherent pulse area, enabling shorter transfer times than the Hermitian benchmark with the same average Rabi frequency. Our work integrates the universal quantum control (UQC) into the biorthogonal representation, displaying full-rank passage engineering with coherent operations in non-Hermitian systems.

In particular, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for extracting the transitionless pathways that transport parallel in ket and bra states. When this condition is satisfied by a set of projectors constructed with biorthogonal basis states, the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian becomes diagonal in the relevant biorthogonal subspace, enabling arbitrary initial state to evolve as a superposition of controlled transitionless passages. We further identify the parametric constraints under which the transformation linking the initial and final states becomes unitary. As a result, the final system state is automatically normalized even though the transitional dynamics is nonunitary. Our theory is justified by the bidirectional population transfer and a holomonic quantum gate implemented by a non-Hermitian three-level system in $\Lambda$ type. For the population transfer, controlled gain and loss reduce the required coherent pulse area, enabling shorter transfer times than the Hermitian benchmark with the same average Rabi frequency. Our work integrates the universal quantum control (UQC) into the biorthogonal representation, displaying full-rank passage engineering with coherent operations in non-Hermitian systems.

items.title: Quantum Advantage in Beam-Displacement Estimation for Inter-Satellite Quantum-Secure Time Transfer
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Ziqing Wang, Robert Malaney
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we investigate the practical feasibility of achieving a quantum advantage, in the context of inter-satellite quantum communication, of satellite position estimation. The investigation focuses on a quantum-enhanced scheme in which squeezing is added to the derivative mode of a Gaussian probe beam as a means of estimating photon-beam displacement. The performance of the scheme is compared against the standard quantum limit achieved by an optimal classical beam-displacement estimation scheme under a fair same-total-energy constraint. We find that although the benefit provided by squeezing rapidly diminishes as the inter-satellite distance increases due to diffraction-induced beam spreading and subsequent truncation by the finite receiver aperture, a quantum advantage can still be expected over inter-satellite distances up to approximately 100 km under practical satellite configurations. This distance scale between satellites is anticipated for Starlink-type satellite constellations.

items.title: Quantum Vehicle Routing Problem: a smart initialization strategy for ill-conditioned optimization landscapes
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Emanuele Casciaro, Mario De Simone, Stefano Martina, Fabio Mascherpa, Alfonso Amendola, Filippo Caruso
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the expansion of complex transport infrastructure, new paths for linking different destinations have emerged, allowing the definition of multiple routes. The introduction of new roads may also lead to disruptions in traffic flow. This problem can be generalized into a special case of VRP, which aims to find the optimal route for a fleet of vehicles within a network of destinations. Finding solutions to this problem requires an exponential number of operations, hindering the ability of exact solvers to deal with large instances, which must therefore be tackled using heuristics, often leading to suboptimal results. Quantum-based algorithms may allow us to find exact solutions in polynomial time with high probability, offering a potential future alternative to classical solvers and in this work, we focus on the QAOA. Our novel contributions are a parameter-initialization strategy that improves the convergence probability and the integration of the subtour constraints directly into the optimization without using additional qubits by employing an approximation of exponential equality constraints. We believe that our results pave the way for effectively solving instances of VRP using quantum-based solutions, leveraging the space-efficient problem encoding and our initialization strategy, which limits the effect of barren-plateau under random parameter initialization.

items.title: Entangled Measurement Outcomes for Optimal Postselection in Quantum Batteries
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Yali Du, Zhipei Zhou, Xiaoli Hu
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Postselection can enhance the performance of a selected quantum battery branch, raising the question of whether the optimum can always be achieved by product measurements on the auxiliary subsystems. For battery auxiliary states obtained by mixing a pure state with global white noise of strength p, the conditional ergotropy reduces to a generalized Rayleigh quotient. For 0<p<1, product postselection attains the joint optimum if and only if the eigenspace associated with the largest generalized eigenvalue contains a product vector. For two auxiliary qubits, a strict product-joint gap therefore occurs precisely when this eigenspace is one dimensional and spanned by an entangled vector. Noisy W and GHZ states display qualitatively different behavior: the three qubit W state exhibits a strict gap throughout 0<p<1, whereas the three qubit GHZ state admits a product optimum. For interacting two qubit batteries, the optimal postselection can switch from a Bell outcome to a product outcome as the coupling strength is varied. By contrast, the outcome averaged capacity and ergotropy are independent of the measurement basis, showing that the joint measurement advantage is genuinely postselective.

items.title: Probing Operator Spreading with Local Quantum Fluctuations
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Bert\'{u}lio de Lima Bernardo
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Measuring out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) is experimentally challenging, often requiring effective reversal of many-body dynamics. Here, we propose an alternative approach to probing operator spreading through local quantum fluctuations, using only forward evolution and local measurements. Motivated by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, we introduce a differential local variance and establish a rigorous bound connecting it to operator noncommutativity. For a ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain in the single-magnon regime, we derive an exact relation between the local variance and a squared-commutator OTOC. In integrable and nonintegrable Ising chains, the differential variance and OTOCs reveal qualitatively consistent propagation fronts. Our results establish local quantum fluctuations as an experimentally accessible, state-dependent, and complementary diagnostic of operator spreading.

items.title: Encoded reversible addition in constant Toffoli depth
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Aidan Epperly, Isaac H. Kim, Mingyu Lee
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that reversible in-place quantum addition modulo $2^n-1$ can be implemented in constant Toffoli depth using $O(n)$ space, provided that the variables are encoded in a certain non-standard form. Using measurement-based uncomputation, the Toffoli depth can be reduced to one. We also present space-depth tradeoffs and an application to programmable rotations.

items.title: Hypergraph cycle enumeration for efficient inference of planted k-XOR with smooth trade-off
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Arman Babakhani, Enrico Fontana, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Ruslan Shaydulin
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce hypergraph cycle enumeration (HCE), a simple spectral framework for detecting and recovering planted signals in noisy hypergraph inference problems. We study HCE on one representative problem from this class, namely planted noisy k-XOR, also known as sparse Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). Both theoretically and empirically, HCE achieves comparable recovery behavior to Kikuchi method, matching Kikuchi hierarchy. We identify parameter regimes where HCE outperforms Kikuchi method, showing that neither algorithm is universally better. We also show a subquadratic quantum speedup for HCE by replacing one of the algorithm's steps with a quantum walk. Our classical and quantum algorithms do not refute the quartic quantum speedup of quantum Kikuchi method, which remains valid for the practically relevant regime of large size and high noise strength.

items.title: Variational Programs with Open Clocks
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Javaria Ghafoor, Amr Sabry
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational quantum algorithms leave the durations of Hamiltonian evolutions open for a classical optimizer to set. We present VHamilton, a minimal extension of the Hamilton quantum programming language in which such durations are open clocks: one program denotes a family of Hamiltonian trajectories, and a valuation fills its clocks with exact dyadic times, so that each instance is an ordinary Hamilton program that compiles to circuits as before. Because the semantics stays exact and affine in the clocks, the Hamiltonian structure of a variational program remainsavail able for reasoning about every valuation at once. Equivalence becomes a finite calculation, which we mechanize in Agda for a fragment and use to prove the VHamilton form of the compiler rewrite "rzz(t) = cx; rz(t); cx" for every clock value. We then show what the same structure supports in a two-qubit chemistry eigensolver written in VHamilton and run through a Haskell prototype. It supports a fusion of commuting blocks, a closed form and an expressibility proof for the ansatz, and an exact split of the error between the precision of the target and that of the clocks, with a priori bounds. It also supports a coordinate search whose queries per sweep, fixed by the spectra of the generators, do not grow with the precision. On the benchmark this search reaches the numerically verified optimum of a grid of 134 million valuations in 53 energy queries. It finds the grid optimum in only 21 of 30 validation settings, however, so the gain is conditional, not a global-optimization guarantee.

items.title: Preparation of a Laughlin-like fractional Chern insulator on a superconducting quantum processor
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Kamil Dutkiewicz, B\'arbara Andrade, Geza Giedke, Tobias Grass
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) are lattice analogues of fractional quantum Hall states, hosting topological order and fractionalized anyonic excitations. Their realization poses a demanding target for quantum simulation. Here, we realize a bosonic FCI on an IBM Nighthawk superconducting quantum processor using classically optimized variational circuits. We target a Laughlin-like state that is an exact zero-energy ground state of a long-range parent Hamiltonian on a torus, eliminating physical edges and providing a favorable geometry for accessing fractional quantum Hall physics in a small system. On a $4\times4$ qubit lattice, we prepare both the four-boson FCI ground state and a three-boson state hosting two quasiholes. Measurements of particle densities and correlations reproduce the characteristic structure of the target states, while reconstructed chiral magnetization currents resolve the circulating current pattern associated with the quasiholes. The preparation of these strongly correlated topological states with shallow circuits establishes a route toward the digital simulation and manipulation of fractionalized excitations, including measurements of topological invariants and anyonic braiding.

items.title: Vacuum amplification across a programmable bosonic Bogoliubov stability boundary in a trapped-ion chain
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Lu Qi, Duanyang Wang, Kenneth R. Brown
items.summary: arXiv:2610.41033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quantum oscillator always carries vacuum fluctuations, and modulating its parameters converts them into correlated pairs of real quanta. This vacuum amplification underlies squeezed light and Hawking radiation. In a closed quadratic system, pair creation competes with the energy splitting of the modes, and growth turns exponential only once pairing overcomes the splitting. Here we realize this competition in two motional modes of a trapped-ion chain. A two-mode-squeezing drive creates the pairs, and a beam-splitter coupling splits the motion into two coupled modes at different frequencies. The two rates are tuned and calibrated independently. Starting near the motional ground state, we cross the stability boundary in two ways. First, with the drive at the sum of the two bare-mode frequencies, the phonon number stays bounded until the pairing rate exceeds the splitting and grows exponentially beyond it. Second, tuning the drive into resonance with one coupled mode lowers the threshold to zero, and only that mode is amplified into a squeezed vacuum. Separate control of the two interactions makes the threshold for vacuum amplification programmable. This control can be used to simulate particle creation and quantum phase transitions, and to operate parametrically driven bosonic devices close to their stability limit.

items.title: Colloquium: Quantum information processing with ensembles of identical particles
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Matteo Piccolini, Marcin Karczewski, Jin-Shi Xu, Chuan-Feng Li, Guang-Can Guo, Giuseppe Compagno, Farzam Nosrati, Rosario Lo Franco
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identical particles underpin most quantum technologies, but the role of indistinguishability in these processes extends far beyond the symmetrization of many-particle states. This Colloquium presents a unified operational perspective on how particle identity, indistinguishability, exchange statistics, and many-particle interference can instead be harnessed as resources for quantum information processing. We first clarify the notions of entanglement and indistinguishability for identical particles, emphasizing their dependence on the accessible measurements and information. We then review how spatial overlap, multiparticle interference, and path identity enable the generation, extraction, protection, and distillation of coherence and entanglement. Their applications to quantum metrology and imaging, state discrimination, teleportation, entanglement swapping, and quantum cloning are examined. Finally, we discuss the thermodynamic role of indistinguishability, from the Gibbs paradox to quantum thermal machines and statistics-driven engines. Across these settings, indistinguishability emerges as a controllable, task-dependent resource whose benefits are determined by state preparation, exchange statistics, interference, and measurement constraints.

items.title: Clifford synthesis is NP-complete
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: S{\o}ren Fuglede J{\o}rgensen
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the problem of synthesizing a quantum circuit for a given Clifford operator using at most a specified amount of resources is NP-complete for several resource models of practical interest. Specifically, we study synthesis of a given Clifford operator using single-qubit Clifford gates and two-qubit Clifford gates, with full qubit connectivity and no additional ancilla qubits. With single-qubit gates free and CNOT as the only two-qubit gate, we show that deciding whether a given target admits an implementation using at most a specified number of CNOT gates is NP-complete, and we show that the problem remains NP-complete when any two-qubit Clifford gate is allowed and the budget counts all such gates. Moreover, we show that both results continue to hold when SWAP gates may be inserted for free, and when single-qubit gates are also considered part of the budget. In each case, we build on recent work by Li and Guan and show that there are polynomial-time reductions from Hamiltonian path in grid graphs to these decision problems, using a number of qubits quadratic in the number of grid vertices.

items.title: Optical Quantum Memory Processing for Quantum Hashing
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: S. A. Moiseev, M. M. Minnegaliev
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sender authentication is an important requirement for secure quantum communication networks. We propose programmable photon-echo quantum memory processing of a multi-time-bin photonic qudit for implementing a quantum-hash-based verification protocol. In this approach, using QM, sender (Alice) generates a quantum hash state by transforming a single stored photonic wave packet into the programmable photonic qudit. Bob's memory coherently maps the received time-bin photonic qudit into a single output mode according to phase encoding. Our scheme relies on a time-resolved coherent detection method introduced here, in which the coherent responses from individual time-bins are sequentially accumulated within Bob's spin coherence prior to the final sender verification. The key advantage of this coherent detection for quantum hashing is shown, and its potential applications are also discussed. The performed analysis demonstrates that experimentally verified parameters of contemporary optical quantum memories enable a proof of principle realization of the proposed architecture. These results reveal an additional role for quantum memories, serving not only as synchronization and repeater resources for long-distance quantum communication, but also as active elements for quantum hashing in conventional quantum key distribution systems.

items.title: Beyond the Kubo formula: unification of adiabatic and isothermal response in quantum systems
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Giuliano Chiriac\`{o}, Vasco Cavina
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The static limit of the Kubo susceptibility describes the adiabatic response of an isolated quantum system, in which energy-level occupations remain unchanged, and generally differs from the isothermal susceptibility, where these occupations readjust to thermal equilibrium. In this work, we introduce a single dynamical framework in which the adiabatic and isothermal responses arise naturally as two distinct limiting regimes. This can be done by considering explicitly an open system version of the Kubo approach in which the dissipation is governed by a typical thermalization rate of the system. By exchanging the order of the static limit and of the vanishing thermalization rate limit, the protocol yields either the adiabatic or isothermal response. This protocol has a solid physical motivation in terms of the thermalization dynamics and is valid for generic systems. We apply it to the case of the magnetic response of the electron gas and reproduce the expected results.

items.title: Witnessing and quantifying stellar rank with the Wigner function
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Oliver Hahn, Alex Maltesson, Varun Upreti, Marike Ellerbroek, Alessandro Ferraro, Saleh Rahimi-Keshari, Ulysse Chabaud, Giulia Ferrini
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying non-Gaussianity is essential for assessing the computational power of bosonic quantum systems. We introduce a framework to witness and quantify non-Gaussianity from displaced parity measurements, and we directly apply it to experimental data obtained with superconducting cavities. Our method estimates fidelities with target pure states from the displaced parity measurements, enabling certification of non-Gaussianity via the stellar rank. We further introduce refined witnesses computed by measuring the value of the Wigner function at a few points, providing efficient certification tools outperforming existing ones. Applying these techniques to Fock, binomial, cat, and GKP experimental data, we rigorously certify non-Gaussian resources and establish a stellar rank of $8$ for a GKP state, setting a new benchmark across all quantum platforms. Our methods enable a rigorous quantification of non-Gaussian quantum resources directly applicable to superconducting devices.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Liangnuo Zhang, Tanner Culpitt, Qiwei Yin, Linghua Zhu, Xiaosong Li
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data encoding is a central challenge in quantum machine learning (QML), as it determines how classical information is mapped onto quantum states and influences the expressive power and efficiency of parameterized quantum circuits. Here, we introduce a physics-informed quantum encoding strategy that exploits the intrinsic many-body structure of electronic systems to establish a direct correspondence between the body order of input descriptors and the locality of quantum gates. Specifically, $n$-body electronic descriptors obtained from a single mean-field electronic-structure calculation are encoded through $n$-qubit gates, yielding a systematic hierarchy of quantum circuits with increasing many-body expressivity. items.title: Predictive Maintenance at the Edge: An Embedded Anomaly Detection Pipeline Trained with Quantum Optimization
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Filipe Chagas Ferraz
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40848v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article presents a predictive-maintenance pipeline that detects anomalies in bearings from vibration signals, adapted for deployment at the edge on low-cost microcontrollers, and that uses quantum optimization in two steps of its training. items.title: A Universal Approach to Hydrodynamics in Higher Dimensions via Tensor Networks
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Sajant Anand, Christopher D. White, Jack Kemp, Julia Wei, Norman Y. Yao, Michael P. Zaletel
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extracting late-time hydrodynamic transport properties directly from microscopic quantum models, especially in dimensions beyond one, is believed to be classically intractable. This owes, in part, to the extensive growth of entanglement in higher dimensions and often a mismatch between geometric and tensor network locality. Here, we extend the Density Matrix Truncation (DMT) algorithm to accurately and quantitatively predict high-temperature transport coefficients (e.g. diffusion constants) in up to three dimensions. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability to capture the slow crossover dynamics characteristic of weakly broken integrability. The intuition underlying our approach is to preserve the geometrically local information crucial for hydrodynamics throughout the time evolution, despite using a one-dimensional matrix product state ansatz for higher-dimensional calculations. Our work pushes the boundary of classical computability and opens the door to benchmarking the high-temperature, late-time dynamics of generic quantum simulators.

items.title: Fock-space delocalization and its control in scarred-vs-ergodic dynamics
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Francesco Perciavalle
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum many-body scarred dynamics in Rydberg-atom arrays is characterized by revivals, in which the system repeatedly returns to its initial state despite its many-body complexity. But how extensively does the wave function explore the space of allowed configurations between revivals? We address this question by quantifying the fraction of configurations occupied during PXP dynamics initialized from the paradigmatic polarized and N\'eel states, which respectively exhibit thermalizing and scarred dynamics. Despite their striking revivals, dynamics from the N\'eel state spreads over exponentially many configurations, yet occupies a vanishing fraction of the full space in the thermodynamic limit. Dynamics from the polarized state, by contrast, occupies a finite fraction of the configuration space, close to anticoncentration and random-state statistics, although chiral symmetry limits this fraction to one third. A weak quasiperiodic field enables the polarized state to occupy half of the configuration space by lifting the constraint imposed by chiral symmetry. The N\'eel state, however, requires a stronger field to reach a comparable anticoncentrated regime. As the field increases further, the occupied fraction decreases for both initial states, revealing a nonmonotonic dependence of Fock-space delocalization on field strength without necessarily implying localization.

items.title: Liouvillian spectral snapshots: A reduced-subspace approach for time-dependent and noisy open quantum systems
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Hans Christiansen, Andr\'e Melo, Jens Paaske, Fabrizio Minganti
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Driven-dissipative quantum devices are routinely operated with time-dependent drives and exposed to temporally correlated classical noise. When these perturbations vary on timescales comparable to the system's intrinsic dynamics, rotating-wave and Markovian approximations can fail, making effective static descriptions unreliable. As a result, accurately modeling systems in this regime often relies on simulating the full time-dependent master equation. This is particularly demanding for processes requiring long integration times, such as rare switching between metastable states, or for stochastic perturbations requiring averaging over many noise realizations. To address these challenges, we introduce Liouvillian spectral snapshots (LSS), a reduced-basis method that enables efficient simulation of such systems by projecting the master equation onto a low-dimensional subspace capturing their coarse-grained dynamics. LSS constructs this subspace by computing the slowly decaying, low-frequency eigenoperators of the Liouvillian at a few adaptively sampled perturbation values and compressing them into a common basis. This basis is built once and can be reused across noise realizations and perturbation parameters, reducing the cost of ensemble averages and parameter sweeps.

items.title: Finite-resource cooling of qudits beyond thermodynamic length
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Ansh Mishra, Aryan Senthilkumar
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cooling a quantum system with $N$ thermal machines costs more than Landauer's bound. For swap-based collision models the excess is set by thermodynamic length, which is optimal for qubits and was suggested by numerics to be optimal in general. We show that for qudits, permutations of energy eigenstates that use several resonant transitions at once do better for every spectrum, reducing the excess by up to 83% near the ground state. To second order, coherent collisions do no better, and at infinite temperature $d_M$-level machines reduce the excess by at most a factor $d_M-1$.

items.title: Quantum manifestations of converse symmetry breaking
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Daniel P. Buser, Biswabibek Bandyopadhyay, Adilson E. Motter
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum synchronization holds promise in advancing quantum technologies such as sensing, communication, and computation. A key challenge in this rapidly developing field is to identify mechanisms that can promote the emergence of synchronous dynamics. Here, we show that quantum synchronization can be enhanced by introducing controlled heterogeneity in the form of coupling mismatches. Using spin van der Pol oscillators as a model system, we show that this mechanism constitutes a quantum analog of the phenomenon of converse symmetry breaking previously identified in classical oscillator networks, where a synchronous state is stabilized by explicit symmetry breaking. We quantify how quantum effects modify this behavior by tuning the degree of quantumness through variations of the spin quantum number. These findings suggest that quantum synchronization can be enhanced in experiments by harnessing rather than suppressing heterogeneity.

items.title: Finite-Element Electromagnetic Analysis and Evaluation of Antenna Performance Metrics Using a Quantum Linear System Solver
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Hiroaki Ominato, Takahiro Ohyama, Shiro Kawabata
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electromagnetic analysis based on the finite element method is widely used in antenna design. At higher frequencies, however, the required mesh refinement makes solving large sparse linear systems the main contributor to computational cost. Quantum linear system solvers offer a potential means of accelerating this step, but their output is a superposition state: reconstructing all components of the classical solution vector would forfeit the quantum speedup. Prior studies have proposed methods for obtaining physical quantities such as scattering cross sections and scattering parameters from the solution state. To support antenna design using fault-tolerant quantum computers, we formulate the total radiated power, the radiated power within a prescribed solid angle, and the dielectric and conductive losses as observables for efficient evaluation from a quantum solution state. These observables avoid the measurement cost of reconstructing all components of the output quantum state. We develop an end-to-end hybrid quantum--classical workflow that combines finite-element electromagnetic analysis, matrix preconditioning, a quantum linear system solver, and the evaluation of antenna design metrics. To validate the workflow, we performed numerical experiments evaluating these observables for an axisymmetric coaxially fed monopole antenna. Under idealized conditions, the relative errors in the total radiated power and the dissipated power with respect to the classical finite-element solution were on the order of $10^{-3}$, confirming the consistency of the workflow. The proposed method is expected to provide a basis for using quantum linear system solvers to evaluate antenna performance and, in the future, to design high-frequency wireless devices.

items.title: Why Testing Structural Theories Requires the Unconscious Condition
items.subtitle: PSYARXIV · 精神分析 · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Zefan Zheng, João Pedro Parreira Rodrigues, Lukas Kob, Karla Matić
items.summary: Consciousness science has traditionally proceeded by contrasting neural activity when a stimulus is consciously perceived against activity when the same stimulus is not perceived. This contrastive approach is well suited to locating neural correlates of consciousness, but it says little about why an experience has the particular character it does. A recent structural turn addresses this gap by comparing the relational structure of qualia with the relational structure of a candidate physical substrate. We review the main structure-matching programmes and what they offer beyond the contrastive approach. We then argue that all of them rest on an assumption that has never been tested directly, which we call the structural exclusivity assumption: That a neural structure matching the qualia structure reflects the neural substrate of consciousness itself, rather than merely the processing of information that can occur without conscious experience. The assumption is empirical rather than philosophical, and the standard structure-matching design cannot test it, because qualia and physical structures are estimated while the content is consciously perceived. We set out the design that would test it, and review the psychophysical and neural evidence currently bearing on it. That evidence consistently suggests that relational structure survives absence of awareness, though no existing study settles the question. We argue that structure-matching and contrastive designs must be combined, and consider what follows for the selection of candidate structures and for the promise of the dissolution of the hard problem of consciousness.

items.title: Unconscious Archetypal Selection Bias in Professional Ice Hockey: A Multivariate Positional Analysis of Astrological Ephemeris Data and the Relative Age Effect
items.subtitle: PSYARXIV · 精神分析 · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: David R. Juillet, Jorge M. Rodrigues, Joanne V. Longtin
items.summary: This study investigates whether unconscious scouting bias exists in National Hockey League (NHL) talent acquisition, driven by psychological and behavioral archetypes. Analyzing a dataset of 777 players across all 32 NHL rosters, the research quantifies standard physical maturity biases, such as the Relative Age Effect (RAE), against independent lunar variables (Sign, Element, Modality) mapped to emotional typologies. Utilizing exact binomial tests, Cohen’s h effect sizes, and Savage-Dickey Bayes Factors (B10), 4,864 distinct positional configurations were evaluated. Results indicate no archetypal solar advantage capable of overcoming the RAE physical penalty. However, when evaluating independent lunar placements across specific positional subgroups (e.g., Centers, Left Wings, Right Wings, Defensemen), extreme localized scouting biases emerge. Front offices consistently filter players through highly distinct, positional psychological profiles, with 13 franchises exhibiting three or more concurrent statistical anomalies, indicating that human evaluation networks unconsciously draft for specific behavioral mechanics.

items.subtitle: PSYARXIV · 精神分析 · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Matthias Pillny, Stefan Leucht, Björn Schlier
items.summary: Montag and colleagues report a randomised trial of modified psychodynamic psychotherapy for schizophrenia (MPP-S) plus treatment as usual (TAU) versus TAU alone. We welcome efforts to strengthen the evidence base for psychodynamic psychotherapy. Given the limited access to psychological treatment for people with psychosis and the, at best, moderate effects of existing pharmacological and psychological interventions this is a valuable effort to advance evidence-based treatment in psychosis. Several methodological decisions, however, complicate interpretation of its findings.

items.title: Representations of Change Support Object Individuation in Infancy
items.subtitle: PSYARXIV · 分析心理学 · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Peter Mazalik, Justin Halberda
items.summary: “One can never step in the same river twice, for it is not the same river and he is not the same man.” This ancient puzzle by Heraclitus highlights that the world, and ourselves, are constantly changing. But to raise these puzzles, one must engage the concept of CHANGE. Developmental research shows that even infants represent highly abstract notions, including objects, agents, cause, and number. Here, we ask whether they also represent CHANGE.We adapted the individuation paradigm pioneered by Xu and Carey (1996), in which two objects emerge sequentially from behind an occluder, preventing spatiotemporal cues about the number of objects. Infants must instead rely on contrastive featural/kind information. Prior work shows that before 12 months, infants fail to individuate objects differing in basic-level category (e.g., duck vs. truck), but succeed with broader distinctions (e.g., object vs. agent).Here we show that infants can use the contrast between a continuously changing object and a static object to infer the number of entities present. This effect cannot beexplained by saliency alone, as infants’ longer looking at unexpected outcomes differsfrom any preference for the more salient changing object, and is striking in light ofreports that infants at this age fail to individuate objects by color alone (Leslie, 1998).Representing change opens a new avenue for research: What types of change areencoded? Over what timescales? Embedded in which cognitive systems? By 8 months,infants already appreciate change as a core property of the world.

items.title: Reframing the Unconscious: A Conceptual Mapping of Jungian Analytical Psychology onto Indian Knowledge Systems
items.subtitle: PSYARXIV · 精神分析 · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Manoj Kumar Mallick
items.summary: Carl Jung engaged Eastern thought throughout his career, writing psychological commentaries on The Secret of the Golden Flower, the Tibetan Book of the Dead, and Kuṇḍalinī yoga, yet this engagement remained impressionistic rather than systematic. No existing review pairs his core constructs with named terms from classical Indian philosophy. This paper proposes a term-by-term conceptual correspondence between six constructs of Jungian analytical psychology and six terms drawn from Sāṃkhya, Patañjali's Yoga, and Advaita Vedānta. It does not introduce a new theoretical model, acronym, or unifying framework. The paper follows Jaakkola's Theory Synthesis template for conceptual articles, distinguished from Theory Adaptation, Typology, and Model approaches. Four criteria guided term selection: definitional precision, scope-matching, textual traceability, and precision over popularity. Each correspondence was checked against primary Jungian texts and established secondary scholarship in Indology. Six correspondences are proposed: Collective Unconscious–Mahat, Archetypes–Tattva, Persona–Vyavahārika, Anima/Animus–Puruṣa/ Prakṛti, Shadow–Kleśa, and Individuation–Svarūpa-bodha. A central divergence emerged alongside these resemblances. Jung's individuation preserves a differentiated, related self, while Advaita's deeper vocabulary points toward non-dual dissolution of that self. This paper treats the divergence as a substantive finding, not a flaw in the method. The mapping offers culturally grounded vocabulary for teaching analytical psychology in Indian settings and for developing culturally resonant counseling language, illustrated through a brief clinical vignette. Risks of essentialism, translation distance, and untested clinical application are named explicitly, with concrete directions proposed for future empirical and textual work.
